title: Changing Your Inner Conversations (leadershipwithatwist.substack.com), September 1, 2026
author: Heather McGonigal
source: Leadership With a Twist (leadershipwithatwist.substack.com), Leadership With a Twist
summary: Leadership coach Heather McGonigal uses the third installment of her Coach Heather Fundamentals series to argue that leaders' internal narratives, not just external events, determine how they respond under pressure. She contends that automatic self-talk — the stories we tell ourselves about a situation, other people, and ourselves — often runs unexamined and directly shapes emotion, communication, and behavior in leadership moments. The piece walks through a simple practice: pause, separate fact from story, then interrogate whether the story being told is actually helping. McGonigal is careful to distinguish this from toxic positivity, framing it instead as increased consciousness of the thoughts driving one's reactions so a leader can choose differently. She closes with a concrete written exercise — naming the story, testing whether it helps, and drafting an alternative — as a way to train the habit over time.
points: The exercise separates observable facts from the interpretive "story" a leader adds on top, since only the story is within their control to revise.
Common unhelpful leadership narratives named in the piece include "they don't respect me," "they should know better," and "I have somehow failed."
McGonigal frames the practice explicitly as building self-awareness and choice, not suppressing genuine feelings or forcing positivity.
Writing the internal narrative down is presented as essential to the practice — externalizing the thought is what makes it possible to question it.
The closing prompt — "Is there anything I could tell myself that might help things go better from here?" — is offered as a reusable habit-forming question for leaders under stress.
quotes: What we tell ourselves matters. Our internal conversations influence how we feel, how we behave, how we communicate, and ultimately what happens next.
After you pause and separate the facts from the story, the next step is to notice the story itself. What are you telling yourself about the situation?
In leadership, our internal narratives can have a tremendous impact. We may tell ourselves someone does not respect us, a team member should know better, a mistake is unacceptable.
Once we can see the story we are telling ourselves, we have more choice about whether we want to keep carrying it forward. That is personal empowerment.

You cannot always control what happens before the pause. You cannot control how another person chooses to behave. But you can become more intentional about the story you carry forward and the person you choose to be within it.
The next time you notice yourself getting emotionally stirred up, take out a piece of paper and write down what you are telling yourself. Get it out of your head and onto the page.
